q: Fill up: Pfannenstiel incision is placed ______ and its feature is ______.
opts: a finger-breadth above the symphysis pubis; cosmetic, rectus muscle not cut
a finger-breadth above the symphysis pubis; poor cosmetic result, rectus muscle cut
3 cm below the ASIS line; cosmetic, rectus muscle not cut
3 cm below the ASIS line; poor cosmetic result, rectus muscle cut

q: Which of the following statements about Joel-Cohen incision compared with Pfannenstiel is TRUE?
opts: Joel-Cohen is straight rather than curved and sited about 3 cm below the line joining the ASIS
Joel-Cohen is curved rather than straight and sited lower close to the symphysis pubis
Joel-Cohen is a vertical midline incision carried down from the umbilicus to the symphysis
Joel-Cohen is a transverse incision placed at the level of the umbilicus with muscle cutting

q: Which of the following statements about transverse skin incision for caesarean is TRUE?
opts: Transverse incision gives less pain, stronger wound and better cosmesis but limits upper abdomen view
Transverse incision gives faster entry but causes more postoperative pain and weaker wound
Transverse incision gives better pelvic exposure though the scar is cosmetically less acceptable
Transverse incision causes less bleeding but results in a mechanically weaker wound postoperatively

q: Match the uterine incision with its description — 1) Sanger's 2) Kerr's 3) Kronig's … A) Classical upper segment vertical B) Lower segment transverse C) Low vertical
Fill up: Risk of scar rupture is ______ for classical caesarean and ______ for one previous LSCS.

Match VBAC eligibility with scar type — 1) Classical 2) One previous LSCS 3) Low vertical (Kronig) … A) Contraindicated B) May be allowed with counselling C) May be allowed, indicated for constriction ring

A 30-year-old woman with a previous classical caesarean at 28 weeks is counselled for the next pregnancy. She is now 36 weeks with no labour pains. What is the most appropriate plan regarding timing and mode?
opts: Repeat caesarean at 36-37 weeks, since contractions become prominent after 37 weeks and raise rupture risk
Trial of labour aiming for vaginal birth at 40 completed weeks with continuous CTG monitoring
Repeat classical section at 39 completed weeks after confirming fetal lung maturity by amniocentesis
Induction of labour at 38 weeks using prostaglandins followed by oxytocin augmentation

q: Which of the following statements about VBAC guidelines after lower segment caesarean is TRUE?
opts: ACOG says a trial may be offered whatever the number of scars; India says contraindicated with two or more
ACOG permits trial after one scar only; Indian guidelines permit trial after any number of scars
ACOG never offers a trial after any scar; India offers trial after two previous sections routinely
ACOG permits trial after three scars; India permits trial after one scar only with mandatory pelvimetry

q: A 27-year-old woman with one previous LSCS at 34 weeks for fetal distress is now 38 weeks, cephalic, with adequate pelvis and no contraindication. She asks about options and success rates. What do you counsel?
opts: Trial of labour succeeds in about 70% or elective repeat caesarean at 39 weeks; avoid prostaglandins
Trial of labour succeeds in about 30% or elective repeat caesarean at 34 weeks with steroids
Elective repeat caesarean at 36 weeks only, since trial of labour is never offered after a scar
Induction with prostaglandins at 38 weeks followed by trial of labour in every woman with a scar

q: All of the following are increased risks associated with trial of labour after caesarean EXCEPT:
opts: Bleeding, need for transfusion, uterine rupture, hysterectomy and fetal distress or death
Transient tachypnoea of the newborn from delayed clearance of fetal lung fluid after caesarean
Severe perineal trauma and anal sphincter injury from vaginal delivery after previous scar
Post-term pregnancy and meconium aspiration syndrome unrelated to mode of delivery

q: All of the following are recognised risks of elective repeat caesarean EXCEPT:
opts: Transient tachypnoea of the newborn, operative and anaesthetic risks and impact on future pregnancies
Uterine rupture in labour and hypoxic-ischaemic encephalopathy from obstructed labour
Severe perineal trauma, pelvic floor dysfunction and anal sphincter injury after vaginal birth
Shoulder dystocia and Erb's palsy from vaginal delivery of a macrosomic fetus

q: Which of the following statements about risk of scar rupture after caesarean is TRUE?
opts: Rupture risk depends on type of previous incision, number of previous caesareans and inter-delivery interval
Rupture risk depends on maternal age alone, which determines tensile strength of the uterine scar
Rupture risk depends on fetal sex and birth weight, since a large baby stretches the scar in labour
Rupture risk depends on placental site alone, because a fundal placenta weakens the lower segment

q: Fill up: Ideal inter-delivery interval after caesarean is ______ months; short interval is ______ months; minimum conception gap is ______ months.
Fill up: Anaesthesia level for painless labour is ______ and for caesarean section is ______.
opts: L1; T6
S2; T8

q: A 26-year-old woman is posted for elective caesarean at 39 weeks for breech presentation. Anaesthetist asks about ideal positioning to prevent supine hypotension. What is the ideal position and timing for non-medical elective CS?
opts: Supine with 15° left lateral tilt; elective caesarean at 39 weeks for non-medical reasons
Supine with 15° left lateral tilt; elective caesarean at 37 weeks to avoid labour onset
Lithotomy position with pelvic wedge; elective caesarean at 39 weeks after lung maturity
Right lateral tilt with wedge under hip; elective caesarean at 40 weeks beyond expected date

q: All of the following are absolute contraindications to VBAC EXCEPT:
opts: Past history of CPD alone without current contracted pelvis or other scar complications
Previous classical caesarean, prior uterine rupture, myomectomy entering cavity or T-shaped incision
Contracted pelvis or cephalopelvic disproportion in the present pregnancy on clinical pelvimetry
Home delivery setting with no facility for emergency caesarean section or blood transfusion

q: Fill up: The most important favourable marker for VBAC is ______ and a bad marker is ______.
opts: previous vaginal delivery; previous puerperal sepsis in the scar
young maternal age; macrosomic fetus in present pregnancy
male fetus; twin pregnancy in present gestation
short maternal stature; post-term pregnancy beyond 40 weeks

q: A 29-year-old woman with one previous LSCS at 38 weeks presents at 39 weeks with Bishop score 4. She desires VBAC and needs induction. What is the recommended method for induction in previous caesarean?
opts: Mechanical cervical ripening with Foley followed by oxytocin; prostaglandins are avoided
Misoprostol 25 mcg vaginally for ripening; oxytocin is avoided due to rupture risk
Dinoprostone gel for cervical ripening; mechanical methods are avoided in scarred uterus
Induction is never attempted after caesarean, so elective repeat caesarean is always performed

q: Match the procedure with its status in previous caesarean — 1) External cephalic version 2) Internal podalic version 3) Contracted pelvis … A) Relative contraindication B) Absolute contraindication C) Recurrent indication for caesarean
All of the following are indications for classical caesarean section (difficult lower segment access) EXCEPT:
opts: Carcinoma cervix, dense bladder adhesions and placenta previa with large vessels over lower segment
Breech presentation, uncomplicated twin pregnancy and macrosomic fetus at term without obstruction
One previous lower segment scar alone with no other complicating factor in present pregnancy
Fetal distress at term and failed induction of labour where lower segment is accessible
